country.name: Tunisia
country.tagline: Carthage's wine country, home of the first great agricultural writer and of Cap Bon's dry Muscat.

stats.note: Wikipedia: about 31,000 ha of vines in 2008, just over half for wine; production 300,000 to 400,000 hl a year in the 2000s. No recent OIV figure.

country.overview:
Tunisia is Carthage, and Carthage wrote the book on viticulture. The Punic agronomist Mago composed a 28-volume treatise on farming, including how to plant and prune vines and how to make passum, raisin wine; when Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, the Senate ordered his work translated into Latin, and Columella, Varro and Pliny quoted it. The Punic town of Kerkouane on Cap Bon, preserved because it was never rebuilt, and Roman villas with wine mosaics (the Bardo museum in Tunis has some of the finest Dionysiac mosaics in the world) show how deeply wine ran through North African life.

After the Arab conquest wine shrank but never vanished, and after the French protectorate began in 1881 large vineyards were planted on the plains around Tunis and on Cap Bon. Seven appellations were created between 1958 and the 1970s and registered internationally under the Lisbon Agreement. Since the late 1990s European investment (from Italy, France and Germany) has modernised a sector that was largely run by state and cooperative wineries.

Tunisian wine is mostly rosé and red from Mediterranean grapes (Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet), with dry and sweet Muscat of Alexandria on the windy tip of Cap Bon at Kélibia as the local speciality. The country sells mostly at home, to tourists and to Germany and France.

history.title: Mago's treatise
history.text: The Carthaginian Mago wrote a 28-book agricultural manual, translated into Latin on the Roman Senate's orders after 146 BC; its fragments include advice on vines and raisin wine.

history.title: Kerkouane
history.text: A Punic town on Cap Bon abandoned around 250 BC and never rebuilt, giving a rare picture of Carthaginian domestic life in the Muscat country of Kélibia.

history.title: The French vineyard
history.text: Under the French protectorate large estates were planted around Tunis, Mornag and Cap Bon, mostly for bulk wine shipped to France.

history.title: Tunisia's AOCs
history.text: Muscat de Kélibia and Muscat de Thibar (1958), then Mornag, Coteaux de Tébourba and Sidi Salem (1973) and others were created as appellations.

country.classification: Tunisia has a French-style system of appellations d'origine contrôlée, with seven names registered under the Lisbon Agreement: Grand Cru Mornag, Mornag, Coteaux de Tébourba, Sidi Salem, Kélibia (Muscat de Kélibia), Thibar (Muscat de Thibar) and Coteaux d'Utique. Labels also use 'Premier Cru' for higher-quality AOC wines.
country.climate_soils: Mediterranean north and Cap Bon with hot summers and winter rain; sandy and clay-limestone soils; the Atlas foothills around Thibar and Bou Arada are higher and cooler.

grapes.name: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet, Merlot

sources.title: Wikipedia, Geographical indications in Tunisia (WIPO Lisbon register)

tn-coteaux-de-tebourba.name: Coteaux de Tébourba
tn-coteaux-de-tebourba.summary: Hills along the Medjerda river west of Tunis around Tébourba, once a centre of French colonial estates. The Medjerda valley's alluvial soils and hillsides give reds and rosés from Carignan and Cinsault, and a little white wine.

tn-coteaux-dutique.name: Coteaux d'Utique
tn-coteaux-dutique.summary: Named after the Phoenician city of Utica, older than Carthage, on the lower Medjerda north-west of Tunis. Vineyards lie on low hills near the ruins of Utica and the coast of the Gulf of Tunis, giving soft reds and rosés.

tn-grand-cru-mornag.name: Grand Cru Mornag
tn-grand-cru-mornag.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cabernet Sauvignon
tn-grand-cru-mornag.summary: The top tier of the Mornag area, from lower-yielding hillside vineyards; 'Grand Cru' is part of the registered name. It sits at the top of the Tunisian hierarchy, and its reds are often oak-aged blends that include Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon alongside the traditional Mediterranean grapes.

tn-kelibia.name: Kélibia
tn-kelibia.summary: Muscat de Kélibia comes from the sandy, windswept tip of Cap Bon around Kélibia, made dry and aromatic (unusually for Muscat of Alexandria) as well as sweet. Kerkouane's Punic ruins lie just north.

tn-mornag.name: Mornag
tn-mornag.summary: The largest Tunisian appellation, on the plain and hills south-east of Tunis around Mornag, Khledia and the slopes of Djebel Ressas. Most of the country's reds and rosés come from here.

tn-sidi-salem.name: Sidi Salem
tn-sidi-salem.summary: A small appellation in the hinterland of Tunis; reds and rosés from Mediterranean varieties. Created in 1973 along with Mornag and Coteaux de Tébourba, it is one of the less-seen Tunisian names on export labels.

tn-thibar.name: Thibar
tn-thibar.summary: Muscat de Thibar comes from the hills of Béja governorate, where the White Fathers missionaries founded a domain in 1895 and made wine and Thibarine liqueur. It is one of Tunisia's two historic Muscat appellations, both created in 1958, alongside Kélibia.

sites.name: Carthage
sites.text: The Phoenician and Punic metropolis whose agronomist Mago wrote the classic treatise on farming and viticulture; destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and rebuilt as a Roman city. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Kerkouane
sites.text: The best-preserved Punic town, on Cap Bon near Kélibia, abandoned in the third century BC and never rebuilt (UNESCO).

sites.name: Domaine Neferis
sites.text: A Tunisian-Italian estate near Grombalia on Cap Bon, one of the modern wineries built since the late 1990s.

sites.name: Domaine Atlas
sites.text: A Tunisian-German estate near Bou Argoub on Cap Bon, one of the private wineries founded after the sector opened to foreign investment in the late 1990s. It makes AOC and Premier Cru reds and rosés from Mediterranean grapes on sandy coastal soils.

sites.name: Kélibia
sites.text: Fishing town at the tip of Cap Bon and centre of AOC Muscat de Kélibia.

sites.name: Thibar
sites.text: Village in the Béja hills where the White Fathers planted vines in the 1890s; home of Muscat de Thibar.

sites.name: Mornag
sites.text: Town on the plain south-east of Tunis at the heart of Tunisia's largest appellation, created in 1973. French colonists planted the area after 1881; today its reds and rosés from Carignan, Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah supply much of the country's wine.
